1:
Why this law stands where it does they explain two ways. Gill reports the Jewish observation that it connects closely with the law of the suspected wife just before, since women are concerned in both, and that, wine leading to adultery, the Nazarite's abstinence and his forbearance of trimming the hair were likely means of preserving from unchastity. Henry makes the link a contrast: after the law for the shame of those who by sin had made themselves vile, fitly follows this for the direction of those who by their piety had made themselves honourable. Who might take the vow Gill fences with the Jewish canon that the Gentiles have no Nazariteship: though they may bring vows and freewill offerings as an Israelite, they are not bound by this law but remain free to drink wine and to defile themselves for the dead, since it is written, speak unto the children of Israel. Wesley adds that both sexes might vow it if they were free and at their own disposal, since otherwise parents or husbands could disannul it.

Whether the institution existed before the law they take differently. Keil holds that the wording shows the vow to have been not only a matter of free choice but a mode of godliness already customary among the people, though its origin is involved in obscurity; he denies any clue that it came from Egypt, since hair-offering vows are met with among several ancient tribes and vows of abstinence were common to all the religions of antiquity. Henry agrees that it is spoken of as a thing already well known, the law only reducing its obligation to a greater certainty. Calvin argues the other way from Amos, that God alone was the appointer of the vow, and that, abominating all fictitious worship, he restrained their licentiousness by giving a clear and certain rule. Ellicott finds the verb remarkable: it denotes the doing of something wonderful or extraordinary, the lesson being that Christ's servants are required to do more than others.

Whether the Nazarite prefigured Christ divides them sharply. Calvin says Samson, sanctified from the womb rather than for a season, was a type of Christ and represented him, and generalises: the nearer anyone under the Law approached to God, the more did Christ shine forth in him. Clarke will have none of it: some contend strongly for the type, but neither analogy nor proof can be produced, since our blessed Lord both drank wine and touched the dead, which no Nazarite would do; and he dismantles the argument from his being called a Nazarene by separating the word for branch, which the prophets do apply to him, from the word for a separated person, which they never do. Henry takes a middle place: Christ was no Nazarite according to this law, for he drank wine and touched dead bodies, yet in him the type had its accomplishment, since in him all purity and perfection met.

What the institution became afterwards Clarke and Henry take in opposite directions. Clarke traces a descent: from the Nazarites sprang the Rechabites, from the Rechabites the Essenes, from the Essenes the Anchorites or Hermits, and in imitation of those the different monastic orders. Henry allows the resemblance to be the only one in Scripture and then denies it point by point: the religious of that church are forbidden to marry, where no such restriction lies on the Nazarite; they abstain from meats, where he might eat any food allowed other Israelites; they are not forbidden wine even on fasting days, where he might have none at any time; and their vow is for life, where his was for a limited time of his own choosing. Calvin's image is gentler: the Nazarites shone among the people like precious jewels, standard-bearers to awaken zeal in the multitude, though few imitated them.
3:
Why the fence runs so far past wine itself they answer in four ways. Calvin makes it a guard against evasion: the simple observance was that they should not drink what inebriates, but because men are crafty in inventing subterfuges it was necessary to specify the means by which the Law might be defrauded, since otherwise they would have kept their luxuries in fresh or dried grapes, or in juice pressed from grapes mixed with water; and he draws the moral, that man's hypocrisy has many lurking-places, shamelessly imagining stupid means of cheating God himself. Wesley puts it more simply, that grapes were forbidden for greater caution, to keep him at the farther distance from wine. Gill takes it of fitness for duty, not merely immoderate drinking being forbidden but drinking at all, that he might be freer for prayer, meditation and the worship of God. Ellicott makes it symbolic, the prohibition of even what does not intoxicate denoting entire consecration and the obligation to abstain from all the delights of the flesh.

Three of them measure the Nazarite against the priest and get three results. Ellicott makes the comparison a contrast: this law, here and in the matter of the dead, was stricter than what was enjoined upon the priests, who were forbidden wine when they entered the tabernacle to serve but not at other times. Calvin makes the same likeness an approach: this similarity proves that the Nazarites were separated from the multitude in order that they might come near the honour of the priesthood. Keil makes it a matter of insignia, the free growth of the hair being called the diadem of his God upon his head, answering to the golden diadem on the high priest's turban and the anointing oil, so that the consecration of the Nazarite culminated in his uncut hair.

How long the vow ran they do not agree. Gill follows the rabbis, that a vow expressed absolutely is understood of thirty days, and that the term might run to a thousand days but never fall below thirty. Clarke reasons from the ceremony instead, holding that it was probably never less than a whole year, so that the man might have a full growth of hair to burn in the fire under the peace-offering. Wesley leaves it open, that the days were sometimes more and sometimes fewer, as he thought fit to appoint. Of the words themselves Clarke says the term rendered vinegar signifies fermented wine, probably here a liquor of strong body; Ellicott reports that strong drink is supposed to have been made of barley and dates or honey, and that of the two words closing the prohibition the first is taken for sour grapes or for the kernels of berries, the second for the shell or husk.

Whether the vow points towards the cloister they answer opposite ways. Ellicott denies it outright: the ideal of this separation was not a life of monastic seclusion but of action, and of uninterrupted devotion to the Divine service. Calvin turns on the monks with heat: boasting angelical perfection, they yet with one accord refuse to abstain from wine, counting it sinful to touch a bit of beef their whole life long and ready to glory in being martyrs rather than eat meat in necessity, while their austerity as to food purchases them the greater licence in drinking, as if they purposely avenged themselves that way. He adds a plainer lesson, that a sober use of wine is a chief part of temperate living, since those who are not abstemious will sooner take common food than bear to be deprived of wine. Clarke reports a conjecture that the Nazarite was the emblem of man in his innocence, and that the vine was forbidden him because the tree of knowledge was itself a vine.
6:
On the dead they all place the Nazarite level with the high priest and above the ordinary one. Gill notes that what even the common priests might do, a Nazarite might not: he could not come near his dead kindred to touch them, to close their eyes, or to attend the funeral. Ellicott states it as a rule, that the law here was equally stringent with the high priest's and stricter than what was imposed on the priests generally; Keil says the same, adding that Samson's mother might eat nothing unclean during her pregnancy; Calvin observes that this too they had in common with the high priest, that they were not even to mourn for their relations. Wesley draws from the parity a conclusion Clarke had refused a few verses earlier, that the Nazarite was here equal to the high priest, being in some sort as eminent a type of Christ, and so justly required to prefer the service of God before affection to his nearest relations.

Why mourning itself should be forbidden Calvin handles carefully. It is not that grief is sinful: if it were sinful to weep and lament when our friends are taken from us, Christ would not have wept at the tomb of Lazarus. But perturbation is always associated with grief, and men in mourning give way to ambition and pomp, and purposely provoke themselves to excess, as though nature did not already carry them further than is right; so the Nazarites could give no example of moderation if they mixed with mourners. He sets the two prohibitions against each other as remedies for opposite diseases: as they were before restrained from daintiness, so now a remedy is applied to sorrow. Why a dead body should defile at all he answers that death represents God's curse, the wages of sin, so that Israel was admonished to beware of dead works; and Gill turns the lesson to spiritual Nazarites, to abstain from the company of sinners dead in trespasses.

The two Hebrew words behind very suddenly produce a flat quarrel. Gill transmits the rabbinic reading, that the Targums render them suddenly through ignorance, a chance matter, while Jarchi interprets the first by violence and the second by error, so that both cases are included. Calvin says the two words come from different roots but are of kindred signification, and that a pair of synonyms is the Hebrew way of expressing a superlative, bringing out how unexpected the death was; in his opinion it is puerile of the Jews to understand the first of a bloody murder and the other of a sudden death. Keil rejects a modern explanation with equal bluntness: the head was shaved not because such uncleanness was more especially caught and retained by the hair, as Knobel fancies, but because the hair was the diadem of his God, the ornament of his condition.

Whether the loss of the elapsed days is just they answer differently. Calvin grants it is no light punishment that a man guilty of no fault should begin his vow afresh, and defends it on two grounds: the consecration was voluntary, so none could complain of a rigour he had laid on himself, and it showed how precious to God is the purity of his worship. Wesley finds a fault after all, telling the man to impute the accident either to his own heedlessness or to God's providence so ordering the matter, possibly for the punishment of his other sins. Of the offerings Gill notes that the two birds were the offering of the poorer sort of childbearing women, Keil that the trespass-offering was a recompense for reinstatement in the former state, and Ellicott that the verb rendered offer means literally to do, its sacrificial sense depending on the context. Clarke, from the hair, makes a married woman a Nazarite for life, separated from all others and joined to one husband.
13:
What the phrase this is the law of the Nazarite attaches to Gill leaves open, allowing that it may look back to what precedes, the things a man is obliged to who vows the vow and what he must do if he is defiled, or forward to what follows, the offerings he must bring and the rites to be observed when he has finished. Keil argues for the second and gives a reason: the directions for release are called the law of the Nazarite because the idea of the vow culminated in the sacrificial festival that terminated the consecration, and it was there that it attained its fullest manifestation. Calvin puts the same moment differently, as the point at which the Nazarites must return to their common life, first placing themselves at the door of the tabernacle and then offering a lamb without spot for a burnt-offering, a ewe-lamb for a sin-offering, and a ram for peace-offerings, with cakes of fine flour mingled with oil, wafers and unleavened bread.

The sin-offering at the close is the difficulty, and Calvin makes the most of it. What it means may be questioned, he says, since expiation was needless for the pure and holy; and he answers that here we clearly perceive that however cheerfully and earnestly men endeavour to offer themselves altogether to God, they never attain the goal of perfection, but are always exposed to God's judgment unless he pardon their sins. From this he turns on the doctrine of supererogation: if ever any such work were pleasing to God, the holiness of the Nazarites, testified to by the Law itself, was worthy of the honour, yet God, when the work is complete, commands them to confess their guilt, and suffers not this service to intrude into the place of merit, but requires of them a sacrifice, that they may borrow from elsewhere what does not belong to themselves, though they appear the most perfect of all men.

Wesley reaches the same conclusion by a shorter road: by the sin-offering the man confessed his miscarriages, notwithstanding the strictness of his vow and all the diligence he could use, and so acknowledged his need of the grace of God in Christ Jesus, whom Wesley calls the true Nazarite. Keil and Ellicott put the offering to a narrower use, making it an expiation for sins committed during the period of consecration, which Keil specifies as the involuntary ones. On the burnt-offering the two agree closely, Keil calling it the embodiment of that surrender of himself, body and soul, to the Lord, on which every act of worship should rest, and Ellicott saying it typified the entire consecration of body, soul and spirit to the Lord. The peace-offering all of them take as thanksgiving: Calvin because they might justly congratulate themselves and celebrate God's goodness when they had discharged their duty, God having vouchsafed them no ordinary honour, and Wesley because God had given the man grace to make, and in some measure to keep, such a vow.

Two smaller observations belong to the same verses. Ellicott notes that the verb rendered offer here is not the one used earlier of the priest's action but a different word meaning literally to bring near, whose cognate noun is the Corban that one Evangelist translates as a gift offered to God. Gill remarks on the basket that unleavened bread was used here as at the consecration of Aaron and his sons, though for peace-offerings of thanksgiving leavened bread was the rule, so that the Nazarite's closing sacrifice follows the pattern of a priestly consecration rather than of an ordinary thank-offering. Wesley sums the whole: the man offered all the three sorts of offerings, that he might so far fulfil all righteousness and profess his obligation to observe the will of God in all things.
18:
Why the shaving had to be done at the door Gill and Wesley answer alike and for the same practical reason. Gill cites the Targum of Jonathan, which puts it outside the tabernacle where the people assembled, and reasons that the act was public so that all might know the Nazariteship was at an end, and no offence be taken at the man's drinking wine or attending funerals. Wesley says the same in fewer words: publicly, that it might be known his vow was ended and he was at liberty in what he had restrained himself from, since otherwise some might have been scandalised at his use of his liberty. Ellicott adds only that the consignment of the hair to the sacrificial fire formed a solemn and suitable termination of the days of his separation.

Why the hair should be burned Clarke explains by an argument from the altar: the Nazarite was himself a kind of sacrifice offered through the whole term of his separation, and since no human flesh or blood could be offered on the altar of the Lord, he offered his hair instead at the close, that hair being the token of his subjection and now reckoned the Lord's property. Keil says the same more briefly, that he handed over and sacrificed to the Lord the hair worn in his honour. Gill adds the rabbinic strictness, that since the hair was consecrated by the vow it could be of no use to himself or others and had to come off entire, Maimonides holding that if two hairs only were left the command of shaving was not kept. Clarke notes besides that the Hindoos let their hair grow through a vow and shave it where the vow was made, and reports the opinion of some that the consecration of hair to a deity was in use among the heathen before Moses, and in nations having no connection with the Jews.

The shoulder given to the priest is an anomaly all of them notice and two of them explain differently. Gill and Wesley agree that this must be the left shoulder, since the right was already the priest's due in every peace-offering, so that here he had both, which was peculiar to this case; and both give the same reason, that the vow being sacred and the man having been enabled to perform it, a greater expression of gratitude was expected of him. Keil grounds it elsewhere: the boiled shoulder was given up symbolically by waving, with a cake and wafer, to indicate that the table-fellowship shadowed forth in every peace-offering took place here in a higher degree. Gill describes the waving itself, the priest putting his hands under the Nazarite's and moving them to and fro, backwards and forwards, upwards and downwards, testifying that all the man had depended on God.

What is added beside that that his hand shall get they take alike, Ellicott and Wesley glossing it of any voluntary offering within the man's ability, and Keil explaining that the sacrifices already named were not separately vowed but contained in the Nazarite vow, beyond which he was free to promise what else he could. Clarke supplies from Maimonides a practice the text does not mention: a man might be a Nazarite on another's behalf by bearing part of the charges, a son might fulfil a vow his father had not lived to accomplish, and one who took half the oblations upon himself might discharge them through whatever Nazarite he chose. He quotes Ainsworth's application, that this explains why Paul, having no vow upon him, could be asked to take four men who had and be at charges with them. Keil closes the release where the text does, with the man drinking wine again, probably at the sacrificial meal, after the Lord had received his share.
22:
Why the blessing follows the Nazarite law Gill declines to settle: it is not easy to tell what the connection is, and he offers only Aben Ezra's suggestion, that Nazarites and priests were alike holy persons. Whether the act is prayer or more they answer at four pitches. Calvin distinguishes: the word to bless is often used of praying for blessings, the common duty of all pious persons, but this rite was an efficacious testimony of God's grace, as if the priests bore from his own mouth the commandment to bless. Keil says it was not to remain a pious wish but to be manifested with all the power of a blessing from God. Henry sets both sides: of himself the priest could only beg a blessing, yet being an intercessor by office, and doing it in the name of him who commands the blessing, his prayer carried a promise. Gill is most deflationary: unless the Lord blesses, in vain do the priests bless, for theirs lies in words and wishes, his in real facts.

Calvin cautions his doctrine: God does not so transfer the office as to resign the right, but after entrusting the ministry claims the accomplishment for himself alone; and Henry reports the Hebrew doctors warning the people not to say, what availeth the blessing of this poor simple priest, since receiving it depends not on the priest but on the holy blessed God. Whether the very words bind they divide over. Wesley says they were not tied to them, since Moses and David and Solomon are afterwards found blessing the people in others. Henry answers that in their other devotions no form was prescribed, but that here, lest the blessing look like their own, God put the very words in their mouths; Clarke goes further, that a prayer God himself puts into our mouth must be right, so that prayer and praise alike should be, so far as may be, in the very words of Scripture. Calvin notes besides that they were to pronounce it audibly and not in an obscure whisper, whence he gathers that they preached God's grace.

What the threefold shape signifies splits them. Henry counts the name Jehovah three times, each with a different accent in the original, and says the Jews themselves think there is a mystery in this, which the New Testament has explained. Gill assigns each person a work: the Father election, the Son redemption, the Spirit regeneration and sealing; Clarke reports that several wise and learned men believe the mystery of the Trinity is not obscurely hinted at here, and distributes the clauses accordingly. Ellicott records that reading as commonly recognised, and gives instead a structural account: three double clauses, the name repeated in each, rising until it culminates in that peace which is the highest gift God can bestow. Keil describes the same architecture, the second member of each pair applying the first to the people, the three gradations unfolding the blessing with ever increasing emphasis.

Peace at the close Calvin takes broadly, since the word signifies not only rest but all prosperity and success, and he embraces the latter sense, though the proper one is not disagreeable to him; Wesley divides it three ways, peace with God, with one's own conscience and with all men. Of putting the name upon Israel Calvin prefers the literal Hebrew to the smoother they shall call upon my name, since God deposits his name with the priests as a pledge of his good will. Gill reports a variant reading of the closing promise, referring the them to the priests, as though God would bless those who bless Israel; Aben Ezra takes it of both. Two of them end where the Gospel does: Henry recalls that the last thing Christ did on earth was to bless his disciples with uplifted hands, and Calvin that Luke shows the rite fulfilled in him.
